note: Techno was born here in the mid-'80s, from a dying car city and a lot of Kraftwerk. Listen for: cold, futuristic synth strings over drum-machine funk.
Just across the river from Detroit. Richie Hawtin grew up here and ran Plus 8 Records from Windsor. Listen for: stripped-back, rubbery acid minimalism.
House music, named after the Warehouse club, and acid house from a second-hand Roland 303; later footwork. Listen for: the squelching 303 and raw drum machines.
Garage house, hard techno from Queens, and decades of everything else. Listen for: swinging, soulful drums.
The Sound of Philadelphia: lush strings and a disco hi-hat, the template for disco.
Stax Records: the house band played tight, dry, organ-and-guitar soul. Listen for: the Hammond organ and the space between notes.
Music City's session players. Listen for: chicken-picking guitars and honking, comedic sax.
The Bakersfield sound: country with Telecaster twang and a rock'n'roll backbeat, against Nashville's polish.
Earl Scruggs grew up near here and invented three-finger banjo picking, the engine of bluegrass.
Second-line rhythm: brass bands and funk that swings from the hips. Listen for: syncopated drums that never sit still.

clips.t: My Feet Can't Fail Me Now

note: Tejano conjunto: German accordion polkas, carried across Texas by Mexican-American players.
Surf rock: Dick Dale played the Rendezvous Ballroom here. Listen for: fast, reverb-drenched tremolo picking.
Not California. The Ventures came from Tacoma, Washington, and taught a generation to play guitar instrumentals.
Montreal's microhouse: thousands of tiny radio samples cut-and-pasted into a groove.
Jalisco is the home of mariachi. Listen for: trumpets, violins and the guitarrón bass.
The Cuban bandleader Pérez Prado made the mambo a worldwide craze from Mexico City.
Nortec: Tijuana producers sampling norteño accordion and banda brass into techno.
Cuban descarga: jam sessions where the bass (tumbao) and percussion lock together.
Ska, then dub: Kingston engineers turned songs inside out with echo and reverb. Listen for: the offbeat skank and a bass you feel.
The steelpan was invented in Trinidad from oil drums in the 1930s–40s.
Bossa nova: samba slowed down, with jazz chords, born in Rio's beach neighbourhoods.
Frevo: Recife's carnival march, fast and brassy, played for acrobatic dancers with umbrellas.
Chicha: Peruvian cumbia played on surf-rock guitars with wah and farfisa. Listen for: twangy melodies over a cumbia shuffle.
Amazonian cumbia: Los Mirlos came from Moyobamba in Peru's jungle and made their guitars sound like birds.
Cumbia's roots: gaita flutes and drums from the Caribbean hills of Colombia.
Tango. Astor Piazzolla's nuevo tango brought in jazz and classical. Listen for: the bandoneón, a squeezebox.
Rave, jungle, garage and dubstep, each from a different postcode. Listen for: chopped breakbeats and sub bass.
East London, where grime was born around 2002. Listen for: cold, square-wave synths at 140 bpm.
Dubstep began in Croydon, around Big Apple Records. Listen for: half-step drums and wobbling sub bass.
LTJ Bukem's Good Looking Records: drum & bass with jazz and ambient pads.
The Essex market town where The Prodigy formed in 1990.
Kent commuter belt. The Hartnoll brothers (Orbital) recorded "Chime" at home.
Bristol's sound systems: trip hop, then drum & bass and dubstep with a dubwise heaviness.
Bleep & bass on Warp Records, about 1990. Listen for: pure sine-wave bleeps and gut-shaking bass.
Leeds is 30 miles from Sheffield. Both of these were early Warp hits made by Leeds kids.
Madchester and the Haçienda, where acid house became British.
Hard, industrial techno: Surgeon, Regis and Downwards.
Glasgow: Slam's Soma label, and later the LuckyMe crew.
The Scottish Highlands: the Great Highland bagpipe. Listen for: the drones under the chanter.
Irish traditional dance music: jigs and reels on fiddle, flute, uilleann pipes and bouzouki.
Galicia, Spain's Celtic corner, has its own bagpipe: the gaita.

clips.t: Alborada de Veiga / Muiñeira de Chantada

note: Andalusia: flamenco guitar. Paco de Lucía came from Algeciras. Listen for: rasgueado strums and handclaps (palmas).
The Portuguese guitar (fado's 12-string), and today the batida of Lisbon's suburbs.
Sardinia's launeddas: a triple-pipe reed instrument, played with circular breathing, that goes back thousands of years.
After the Wall fell, techno moved into the empty East: Tresor, Basic Channel's dub techno, Berghain.
Kraftwerk and Neu!: the motorik beat and the Kling Klang studio.
Kompakt Records and the 'Sound of Cologne': minimal techno with a pop heart.
Sven Väth's Omen club and the Harthouse/Eye Q trance labels.
Giorgio Moroder's Musicland studios: sequencer-driven Eurodisco.
The Dial label: melancholy, melodic minimal.
Gabber: Rotterdam's answer to Amsterdam's house. Listen for: distorted kicks at 180+ bpm.
The Hague's electro and Italo-worshipping underground: the Bunker and Viewlexx crews.
Antwerp: new beat and the R&S-era hard techno.
French touch: filtered disco loops, then Ed Banger's distorted electro.
The royal suburb west of Paris produced Air.
Kruder & Dorfmeister's downtempo dub and the G-Stone label.
Loop techno (Drumcode) and The Field's shoegaze techno.
Uppland is the home of the nyckelharpa, a keyed fiddle with resonating strings.
Lindstrøm and Prins Thomas's cosmic space disco.
A small town near Drammen, home of Todd Terje.
The 'Bergen Wave' of the early 2000s: Röyksopp's melodic electronica.
The Hardanger fiddle (hardingfele) has sympathetic strings under the bowed ones. Listen for: a shimmering, droning halo.
Trentemøller's dark, cinematic minimal.
Darude and producer JS16 made the most-memed trance track of all time here.
A village in Romanian Moldavia, home of Fanfare Ciocărlia. Listen for: breakneck Balkan brass in odd meters.
Southern Serbia's Roma brass bands, which own the Guča trumpet festival.
Bulgarian wedding music: Ivo Papasov's clarinet, playing jazz-fast lines in 7/8 and 11/8.
The bouzouki and the sirtaki, written for the film Zorba the Greek. Listen for: it speeding up and up.
Anatolian rock: Turkish folk melodies played on fuzz guitars and organs in the early '70s.
Omar Khorshid's electric guitar playing Arabic maqam scales, a '70s belly-dance and cinema sound.
Munir Bashir, the 'prince of the oud', and the Iraqi maqam.
The santur, a hammered dulcimer at the heart of Persian classical music.
Ethio-jazz: Mulatu Astatke fused Ethiopian scales with Latin jazz and funk. Listen for: the strange, five-note minor scales.
The kora, the 21-string harp-lute of the West African griots. Listen for: a bassline, melody and runs played all at once.
Konono Nº1: thumb pianos (likembé) electrified through homemade mics and old car parts.
The valiha, Madagascar's bamboo tube zither.
Gqom: raw, broken, bass-heavy club music from Durban's townships.
DJ Mujava's 'Township Funk', from Atteridgeville outside Pretoria.
Hindustani classical music. Ravi Shankar was born in Varanasi. Listen for: the sitar's buzzing resonance over a tanpura drone, and tabla.
Carnatic (South Indian) classical music. U. Srinivas played it on electric mandolin.
Molam, the music of northeast Thailand. Listen for: the phin (an electric lute) and the khaen (a bamboo mouth organ).
The đàn bầu: a one-string zither that bends notes like a voice.
The blind street musician Abing composed "Erquan Yingyue" (The Moon Reflected in Second Spring) here. The erhu is a two-string fiddle.
The morin khuur, a horsehead fiddle, plays the sound of galloping horses across the steppe.
Gayageum sanjo: a 12-string zither, starting slow and accelerating.
Koto music: "Rokudan no Shirabe", attributed to the 17th-century Kyoto master Yatsuhashi Kengyō.
Yellow Magic Orchestra wrote the synth-pop playbook; Tokyo's techno producers followed.
Balinese gong kebyar: shimmering, explosive gamelan, with paired instruments tuned slightly apart so they beat.
Javanese court gamelan: slow, stately and meditative, the opposite of Bali's fireworks.
The Hawaiian steel guitar, invented in Hawaii in the 1880s. Listen for: sliding, crying notes.
Israeli psytrance: Goa trance's sound made huge.
The Avalanches built their debut from thousands of samples.
Future Classic and Flume's warped, wobbly synths.
Lucho Bermúdez, from this town in Colombia's Caribbean hills, put coastal cumbia and porro in a big band and took it to Bogotá's ballrooms. Listen for: clarinets over a cumbia shuffle.
